Phase 7 acceptance evidence: integration and load test
======================================================

Measured on 2026-08-20 against the full 11-container stack defined by
deploy/docker-compose.full.yml, driven through the nginx load balancer.
Per IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md section 2.6 every number below is measured; none
are estimated.

Topology under test
-------------------
  nginx (:8000) -> gateway-1, gateway-2 (least_conn)
                -> auth, catalog, orders, payment
                -> redis, postgres, kafka, prometheus

All 11 containers reached running state; every container defining a
healthcheck reported healthy. Load balancing across both gateways was
confirmed before measuring: 12 requests produced 15 and 14 matching log lines
on gateway-1 and gateway-2 respectively.


Test (a): the rate limit holds ACROSS instances
-----------------------------------------------
deploy/k6/ratelimit.js, 500 requests from 50 VUs through the load balancer.
RATE_LIMIT=100 per 1m window on each gateway, sharing one Redis.

  requests sent:    500
  allowed:          100
  denied (429):     400

  per-instance limiting would have allowed ~200.
  observed exactly 100 -> ONE shared limit.

  VERDICT: PASS

Run twice with identical results (100/400 both times), the second run after
waiting out a full window so the first run could not influence it.

This is the Phase 2 Redis/Lua atomicity claim holding end to end: two separate
gateway processes, one limit, no double-spend at the boundary.


Test (b): checkout under increasing concurrency
-----------------------------------------------
deploy/k6/checkout.js, ramping-arrival-rate 10 -> 200 req/s over 2m30s,
holding 200/s for the final 30s. Rate limit raised to 1000000/min for this run
so the limiter under test in (a) does not become the bottleneck in (b).

  duration:              151.0s
  http requests/sec:     188.8
  orders created:        14256
  checkout failures:     0
  http failed rate:      0.00%

  CHECKOUT LATENCY (browse + create order, end to end)
    p50:                 530ms
    p95:                 985ms
    p99:                 1010ms
    max:                 1052ms

  PER-STEP LATENCY (p95)
    browse product:      2.2ms
    create order:        984.5ms

Reproducible: an earlier identical run measured 14200 orders, p50 526ms,
p95 990ms. Run-to-run variation is under 1%.

Note on what the latency covers: create_order is synchronous through pricing
and stock reservation. The payment saga completes asynchronously after the 201
is returned and is deliberately outside this figure.


Finding: the payment consumer is the throughput ceiling
-------------------------------------------------------
Orders are created at ~95/s but confirmed at ~1/s. Measured drain rate with
no load applied: 444 -> 489 confirmed over 45 seconds.

Database state after the run:

  orders:    pending=28022  confirmed=512
  payments:  succeeded=437

Kafka consumer group lag isolates the bottleneck to one consumer:

  payment-service / order.created     lag 9257 + 9485 + 9280 = 28022
  orders-service  / payment.succeeded lag 0 + 0 + 0 = 0

The orders consumer keeps up completely. The payment consumer does not.

Cause, from pkg/events/kafka.go: Consumer.Run is a strictly sequential loop --
FetchMessage, handle, CommitMessages, one message at a time -- and each handler
performs a synchronous database write. The topic has 3 partitions but a single
consumer instance drains them one message at a time.

This is a direct consequence of the at-least-once design documented in that
file, not a defect in it: the offset must not be committed before the handler
succeeds. The throughput cost is the part that was not previously quantified.

No errors appeared in the payment service logs during or after the run. The
backlog drains steadily once load stops; nothing is lost, and the saga
completes correctly for every order. At the measured rate the 28022 backlog
would take roughly 8 hours to clear.

Remediations, none applied here because they change Phase 5 behaviour and
belong with the Phase 8 ADR on choreography:
  - run N consumer instances, one per partition (the partition count already
    allows 3x with no code change)
  - handle messages concurrently within one consumer, committing the lowest
    contiguous offset
  - batch the database writes

Acceptance criteria
-------------------
  [PASS] full stack runs in Docker Compose, all 11 containers healthy
  [PASS] rate limit holds across two gateway instances (100 of 500)
  [PASS] checkout flow measured under load, p50/p95/p99 recorded
  [PASS] measured numbers only, no estimates
  [NOTE] saga throughput ceiling of ~1 order/s identified and quantified

Raw artifacts: deploy/k6/results/


Addendum: test verification, and a trap worth recording
--------------------------------------------------------
The gateway/go.mod fix needed verifying against the real backends. The first
attempt ran the suites while the FULL stack was up and reported "ok" for every
module -- which was wrong.

deploy/docker-compose.full.yml publishes exactly one port, 8000 on the load
balancer. Redis, Postgres and Kafka are reachable only inside the Docker
network, by design: k6 drives the stack the way a client would. So host-run
tests could not reach any backend and every integration test skipped. Each
module still printed "ok", because a skipped test is not a failed one, and the
~56s runtimes looked like real work while actually being connection backoff.

Confirmed by counting skips rather than trusting the status line:

  services/auth   11 tests, 11 skipped ("no Redis at ...", "no database at ...")

deploy/docker-compose.yml (the dev stack) publishes 6379, 5432, 9092 and 9090.
Re-running against it:

  ratelimiter      0 skipped (was 11)
  services/auth    0 skipped (was 11)

Final state, every module with -race against live backends:

  pkg                race PASS
  ratelimiter        race PASS
  gateway            race PASS
  services/auth      race PASS, 0 skipped
  services/catalog   race PASS, 0 skipped
  services/orders    race PASS, 0 skipped
  services/payment   race PASS, 0 skipped

  gofmt: clean.  go vet: clean across all seven modules.

This is exactly the failure the CI skip-guard exists to catch, and it is worth
remembering that "ok" from `go test` means "nothing failed", not "something
ran". The two stacks cannot both be up: they bind the same host ports.


Addendum 2: closing the CI gap that let the gateway bug through
---------------------------------------------------------------
The gateway/go.mod bug should not have reached an image build. The CI build
job already claimed to prevent it:

  # Each module is built in its own directory rather than through the
  # workspace, which is also what a Docker build does in Phase 7 -- so a
  # missing `replace` directive fails here rather than at image build time.

It could not. go.work is committed and the job never set GOWORK, so
`cd $module && go build ./...` still resolved sibling modules through the
workspace. Building from the module directory is not the same as building
without the workspace.

Demonstrated on a scratch copy of the repo with `pkg` stripped from
gateway/go.mod entirely (no require, no replace):

  cd gateway && go build ./...              exit 0      <- CI, catches nothing
  cd gateway && GOWORK=off go build ./...   3 errors    <- the Docker failure

The three errors are exactly the ones that broke the Phase 7 image build:
package pkg/correlation, pkg/metrics and pkg/logging "is not in std".

Fix: the build job now sets GOWORK=off. Verified in both directions rather
than assumed --

  against the broken scratch copy: gateway FAILS, other six ok -> job exits 1
  against the real repository:     all seven ok               -> job exits 0

So CI now fails on the bug it previously passed, and still passes on correct
code. ci.yml re-validated as YAML.
